8. Choosing an output format

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-08-outputs.Rmd
book-08-outputs.Rmd

What you will learn

Choose a table shape for your question and run one small example of every format, including explicit survival censoring.

This chapter uses the public synthetic Synthea27Nj numeric connection from Getting started.

You need: the packages and the matching practice connection described in Before you start. Run its sections in order. Each chapter starts from a fresh practice connection; all the outputs below come from real dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.4 calls. The numbers describe teaching data, not clinical findings.

Start this chapter

Start a fresh R session in the book-work directory created in Getting started. Run this setup first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/connection.R")
source("tools/book/practice.R")
practice <- if (book_driver == "DSLite") book_practice("numeric") else book_connect("numeric")
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
#> [1] "site"

The site connection is ready. The shared connection.R selects DSLite or Opal and resolves the resource names.

Choose the shape for the analysis

An output controls the shape of a private server table. It never grants a row download. Grain means what one row represents: a person, an indexed episode, an event or a time period. More rows do not create more independent people.

Format Use it for Main row meaning
wide A few named variables, models Person or episode
long Event sequences Event within a population episode
features A feature table preset Wide person or episode
baseline Entry characteristics preset Wide person or episode
person_period / panel Repeated measurements over follow-up Episode and time bin
temporal_covariates Sparse changes over time Nonzero covariate and time bin
survival Time until an outcome or censoring Follow-up record
intervals Exposure or event spans Interval
sparse Many mostly absent covariates Nonzero covariate
membership Reuse population episodes Population member episode
dictionary Describe concepts used by outputs Vocabulary entry
joined Combine compatible private outputs Declared join grain

features and baseline are type presets which lower to native wide outputs; panel is the simple-layer name for person_period. We check every resulting recipe selects language 2. Use format for the native formats.

Prepare one small study

We will reuse these definitions so each example changes only the output.

visits <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = c(9201L, 9202L), name = "visits")
rx <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = c(9201L, 9202L), name = "spans")
inpatient <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = 9201L, name = "inpatient")
visitors <- omop_population("visitors", index = omop_index(visits))
class(visitors)
#> [1] "omop_population" "list"

Each first visit begins one episode. A later inpatient visit will be our outcome.

base <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, rx, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = list(
    visits = omop_variable(event = visits, reducer = omop_reduce("count")),
    age = omop_age(),
    hemoglobin = omop_mean_value("measurement", 3000963L, unit = 8713L,
      window = omop_window(NULL, NULL))),
  outputs = omop_output("wide", rows = "visitors", format = "wide"))
recipe_explain(base)$selected
#> [1] "v2"

The visit count reads all history here. Age uses annual year subtraction at entry. The template already contains an executable wide output.

Wide: named columns 

stopifnot(recipe_explain(base, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(base, out = c(wide = "D_fmt_wide"), conns = conns))
#>         wide 
#> "D_fmt_wide"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_wide", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"        "cohort_row_id" "person_id"     "visits"        "age"          
#> [6] "hemoglobin"

There is one row per episode and one column per requested variable. A person’s pseudonym and episode keys are supplied by the server.

Long: keep event records

Use long when event order and repeated records matter. Select a named source instead of reducing it.

long <- base
long$outputs <- list(long = omop_output("long", rows = "visitors", format = "long",
  sources = "visits"))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(long, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(long, out = c(long = "D_fmt_long"), conns = conns))
#>         long 
#> "D_fmt_long"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_long", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"                   "cohort_row_id"            "person_id"               
#> [4] "concept_id"               "start_date"               "end_date"                
#> [7] "visit_type_concept_id"    "admitted_from_concept_id" "discharged_to_concept_id"

The source columns become a normalised schema, including concept_id and start_date. Dates default to offsets from the index. One source makes the event-row meaning clear; multiple sources need an explicit event-log design.

Features: a wide preset

Use the features preset when a downstream analysis expects a feature table. Native typed variables preserve their declared values.

features <- base
features$outputs <- list(features = omop_output("features", rows = "visitors", type = "features"))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(features, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(features, out = c(features = "D_fmt_features"), conns = conns))
#>         features 
#> "D_fmt_features"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_features", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"        "cohort_row_id" "person_id"     "visits"        "age"          
#> [6] "hemoglobin"

This is a wide table, not the sparse coordinate representation shown below. The native selection check prevents an accidental older-language execution.

Baseline: characteristics at entry

Use baseline to name an entry-characteristics table. Define the time windows of its variables explicitly.

baseline <- base
baseline$outputs <- list(baseline = omop_output("baseline", rows = "visitors", type = "baseline"))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(baseline, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(baseline, out = c(baseline = "D_fmt_baseline"), conns = conns))
#>         baseline 
#> "D_fmt_baseline"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_baseline", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"        "cohort_row_id" "person_id"     "visits"        "age"          
#> [6] "hemoglobin"

The preset does not turn an all-history count into a pre-index count. Here the omop_age() baseline preset uses its banded annual-age default. Use omop_age_at() in a wide table for explicit completed age. The simple study layer makes baseline an ordinary wide output.

Panels: one row per follow-up bin

A bin is a time interval. These are three 30-day bins after entry, not calendar months.

panel <- base
panel$outputs <- list(panel = omop_output("panel", rows = "visitors", format = "person_period",
  options = list(sources = list(visits), bins = list(width = 30L),
    window = omop_window(1, 90), analyses = "count", representation = "dense")))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(panel, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(panel, out = c(panel = "D_fmt_panel"), conns = conns))
#>         panel 
#> "D_fmt_panel"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_panel", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"                        "cohort_row_id"                
#> [3] "person_id"                     "period_start_days"            
#> [5] "period_end_days"               "days"                         
#> [7] "visits_inpatient_visit_count"  "visits_outpatient_visit_count"

A dense panel retains the empty bins with zero event counts. bins = list(calendar = "month") instead aligns to calendar months, whose lengths vary. Account for repeated rows per person in downstream analysis.

Temporal covariates: sparse time bins

Use temporal covariates when you need nonzero covariate values with a time index. Including day zero gives this example actual nonzero entries.

temporal <- base
temporal$outputs <- list(temporal = omop_output("temporal", rows = "visitors", format = "temporal_covariates",
  options = list(sources = list(visits), bin_width = 30L,
    window = omop_window(0, 89), analyses = "count")))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(temporal, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(temporal, out = c(temporal = "D_fmt_temporal"), conns = conns))
#> $site
#> $site$temporal
#> $site$temporal$temporal
#> $site$temporal$temporal$symbol
#> [1] "D_fmt_temporal"
#> 
#> $site$temporal$temporal$grain
#> [1] "episode"
#> 
#> $site$temporal$temporal$n_columns
#> [1] 6
#> 
#> 
#> $site$temporal$covariateRef
#> $site$temporal$covariateRef$symbol
#> [1] "D_fmt_temporal.covariateRef"
#> 
#> $site$temporal$covariateRef$grain
#> [1] "none"
#> 
#> $site$temporal$covariateRef$n_columns
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> 
#> $site$temporal$timeRef
#> $site$temporal$timeRef$symbol
#> [1] "D_fmt_temporal.timeRef"
#> 
#> $site$temporal$timeRef$grain
#> [1] "none"
#> 
#> $site$temporal$timeRef$n_columns
#> [1] 3
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_temporal", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"          "cohort_row_id"   "person_id"       "time_id"        
#> [5] "covariate_id"    "covariate_value"

The returned mapping also names the covariate and time reference tables. Keep those companions: numeric covariate/time keys need their definitions. Missing records and missing measurements are not automatically interchangeable.

Survival: state the censoring rule

A time-at-risk window says when outcomes count. Censoring ends follow-up without recording the outcome. Here follow-up starts the day after entry and has no fixed upper limit.

survival <- base
survival$outputs <- list(survival = omop_output("survival", rows = "visitors", format = "survival",
  options = list(outcomes = list(admission = inpatient),
    tar = omop_window(1, NULL), censor = list("observation_end", "death"))))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(survival, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(survival, out = c(survival = "D_fmt_survival"), conns = conns))
#>         survival 
#> "D_fmt_survival"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_survival", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"                "cohort_row_id"         "person_id"            
#> [4] "outcome_name"          "event"                 "entry_days_from_index"
#> [7] "exit_days_from_index"  "follow_up_days"

Only the named censor sources cap follow-up: observation end and death here. The window also limits follow-up when its upper bound is finite. An episode end is not an extra censor unless requested. A censor is not a “no outcome ever” assertion. Always state the window: omitting it would use the 730-day compatibility default.

survival_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_fmt_survival$event", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(survival_result))
Category Count
0 21
1 7

Full aggregate response

survival_result
#> $output.list
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_row.props
#>                     study
#> D_fmt_survival$event site
#>                    0    1
#>                    1    1
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_col.props
#>                     study
#> D_fmt_survival$event site
#>                    0 0.75
#>                    1 0.25
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
#>                     study
#> D_fmt_survival$event site
#>                    0   21
#>                    1    7
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_proportions
#> D_fmt_survival$event
#>    0    1 
#> 0.75 0.25 
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_fmt_survival$event
#>  0  1 
#> 21  7 
#> 
#> 
#> $validity.message
#> [1] "Data in all studies were valid"

Counts of the event flag distinguish observed outcomes from censored follow-up in this one-outcome example.

Intervals: keep a start and an end

Use intervals for recorded spans. These visit intervals have recorded start and end dates. The same layout can describe drug exposures or eras.

intervals <- base
intervals$outputs <- list(intervals = omop_output("intervals", rows = "visitors", format = "intervals",
  options = list(sources = list(rx), window = omop_window(0, NULL))))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(intervals, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(intervals, out = c(intervals = "D_fmt_intervals"), conns = conns))
#>         intervals 
#> "D_fmt_intervals"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_intervals", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"                "cohort_row_id"         "person_id"            
#> [4] "interval_type"         "concept_id"            "start_days_from_index"
#> [7] "end_days_from_index"

Both bounds remain private, normally as index-relative days. Overlapping intervals are not automatically a union of covered days; define an era or a coverage reducer for that question.

Sparse: nonzero covariates plus a reference

Use sparse for many covariates when most combinations have no contribution.

sparse <- base
sparse$outputs <- list(sparse = omop_output("sparse", rows = "visitors", format = "sparse",
  options = list(sources = list(visits), analyses = c("binary", "count"))))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(sparse, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(sparse, out = c(sparse = "D_fmt_sparse"), conns = conns))
#> $site
#> $site$sparse
#> $site$sparse$sparse
#> $site$sparse$sparse$symbol
#> [1] "D_fmt_sparse"
#> 
#> $site$sparse$sparse$grain
#> [1] "episode"
#> 
#> $site$sparse$sparse$n_columns
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> 
#> $site$sparse$covariateRef
#> $site$sparse$covariateRef$symbol
#> [1] "D_fmt_sparse.covariateRef"
#> 
#> $site$sparse$covariateRef$grain
#> [1] "none"
#> 
#> $site$sparse$covariateRef$n_columns
#> [1] 5
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_sparse", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"          "cohort_row_id"   "person_id"       "covariate_id"   
#> [5] "covariate_value"

The data contain a covariate key and value. The reference companion maps keys to source, concept and analysis. A missing sparse row is not a missing person roster: retain membership separately. Each published patient component must meet its own support rule.

Membership: retain the population roster

Use membership to keep entry/end dates and keys for every episode independently of its measurements.

membership <- base
membership$outputs <- list(membership = omop_output("membership", rows = "visitors", format = "membership"))
stopifnot(recipe_explain(membership, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(membership, out = c(membership = "D_fmt_membership"), conns = conns))
#>         membership 
#> "D_fmt_membership"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_membership", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"            "cohort_row_id"     "person_id"         "cohort_start_date"
#> [5] "cohort_end_date"   "index_source"

This is still a patient-linked private object. It is not a public list of participants.

Dictionary: describe the concepts

Use dictionary to describe vocabulary concepts used by a declared source output. Here counts defines those dependencies privately; only the dictionary is published. It does not contain patient rows.

dictionary <- base
dictionary$outputs <- list(
  counts = omop_output("counts", rows = "visitors", format = "wide", columns = "visits"),
  dictionary = omop_output("dictionary", rows = "visitors", format = "dictionary",
    options = list(source_outputs = "counts")))
dictionary$publish <- "dictionary"
stopifnot(recipe_explain(dictionary, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(dictionary, out = c(dictionary = "D_fmt_dictionary"), conns = conns))
#>         dictionary 
#> "D_fmt_dictionary"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_dictionary", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "concept_id"       "concept_name"     "domain_id"        "vocabulary_id"   
#> [5] "concept_class_id" "source"

The schema contains vocabulary fields, not frequencies. A dictionary does not certify that a concept occurred in a particular person, and it is not a replacement for the sparse covariate reference.

Joined: combine private outputs

A native joined output combines declared output dependencies, using their protected keys and a checked cardinality. It is not an arbitrary database join. Keep input columns disjoint and state how many rows can match.

joined <- base
joined$outputs <- list(
  counts = omop_output("counts", rows = "visitors", format = "wide", columns = "visits"),
  ages = omop_output("ages", rows = "visitors", format = "wide", columns = "age"),
  joined = omop_output("joined", rows = "visitors", format = "joined",
    options = list(from = list(list(output = "counts"), list(output = "ages")),
      how = "left", cardinality = "one_to_one")))
joined$publish <- "joined"
recipe_explain(joined)$selected
#> [1] "v2"

Only the final joined output is published. The two input outputs are private intermediate steps and do not each need a separately published symbol.

stopifnot(recipe_explain(joined, conns = conns)$selected == "v2")
print(recipe_execute(joined, out = c(joined = "D_fmt_joined"), conns = conns))
#>         joined 
#> "D_fmt_joined"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_fmt_joined", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"        "cohort_row_id" "person_id"     "visits"        "age"

A left join retains the first input’s rows. Here each episode has exactly one counts row and one ages row. Repeated event rows would require a different, explicit cardinality; do not silently multiply a study population.

Recap

Choose the population and row meaning before the format. Outputs stay private; multi-component outputs carry reference companions. Censoring and join cardinality are study decisions.

Try it

Summarise the visit-count column of the joined output. Why is it the same as the wide count?

Solution

solution_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_fmt_joined$visits", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(solution_result))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 11.75000
site 10% 16.40000
site 25% 23.75000
site 50% 45.00000
site 75% 75.25000
site 90% 117.60000
site 95% 152.20000
site Mean 61.96429

Full aggregate response

solution_result
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean 
#>  11.75000  16.40000  23.75000  45.00000  75.25000 117.60000 152.20000  61.96429

Both use the same reducer and episodes. Joining one row to one row adds a column without duplicating those counts.

Another numeric exercise

Summarise the person-level hemoglobin mean in the wide output. Would an average of a long table’s measurement rows give each person equal weight?

Solution

output_lab <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_fmt_wide$hemoglobin", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(output_lab))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 12.90500
site 10% 13.14667
site 25% 13.78500
site 50% 14.32500
site 75% 15.33542
site 90% 15.70000
site 95% 15.92375
site Mean 14.46679

The wide table gives each included person one mean in g/dL. An average over measurement rows would give more weight to people with more measurements. Working with lab values builds this distinction into a two-connection analysis. Neither shape grants access to individual rows.

Chapter 16 develops these choices through irregular measurements, server reshaping, a discrete-time hazard and pooled mixed models.
